text.t: Myosin is a molecular motor that powers every movement your muscles make, from blinking to each heartbeat.
This file is only the head of a scallop muscle myosin; the long tail was clipped off so it could be studied.
Chain A is the heavy chain, and it holds most of the motor domain, the part that makes the power stroke.
Myosin catches ATP here and splits it into ADP and phosphate.
This crystal caught it holding ADP and a magnesium ion.
Two small light chains ride along with the heavy chain: chain Y is the regulatory light chain and chain Z the essential light chain.
When phosphate leaves, a converter part swings and a long lever arm amplifies the motion into a power stroke.
In this structure the converter and lever arm sit in a new position, likely a stage before ATP is split, when the head stays detached from actin.

does.t: Myosin turns the chemical energy in ATP into movement.
Its heads grab actin filaments and pull them, forming cross-bridges that make a muscle shorten.
About 2 trillion myosin molecules working together are needed to hold up a baseball.

shape.t: Splitting ATP cocks the head into a bent, ready position.
The bent head grabs actin, and the release of phosphate snaps it straight, pushing along the filament.
A new ATP then binds and the head lets go of actin, ready for the next stroke.

text.t: In muscle cells about 300 myosin molecules bundle their tails into a thick filament, with the heads sticking out toward the actin filaments.
Actin and myosin are plentiful in muscle cells, and muscles contract when their filaments slide past each other.

history.who: A. Houdusse, V.N. Kalabokis, D. Himmel, A.G. Szent-Gyorgyi and C. Cohen

text.t: This scallop myosin head with MgADP was solved by X-ray crystallography at 2.5 angstroms.
It showed a new shape of the myosin head, different from earlier structures before and after the power stroke.

compare.t: This myosin head with its two light chains is about 17.4 nm from end to end, the longest protein file in this gallery.
A whole myosin is much larger, with a long tail added to this head.

text.t: The ADP left after ATP is split.
A magnesium ion sits with the ADP in the fuel site.
